name: Daria Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, fifty-eight, an experienced electrician doing ordinary home and shop repairs. I've a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I'm about average at the trade, not a master electrician or a crew lead. Yesterday a landing light kept failing because of a damaged switch; I found the cause, repaired it and tested the circuit within my licence. I like explaining a clear fault, and dislike a customer call after supper that never appears anywhere on the paid record.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like outside the repairs, and how do you approach new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leif is a hospital porter, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent a flat with a very small balcony. My firm pays above the usual electrical wage, both wages cover our costs with room left and we've fourteen months of expenses saved, with plenty of other electrical firms nearby. I occasionally use an AI wording aid after a colleague has shown it works, removing customer details and checking the explanation against the actual repair. I'm a union member who wants saved time shared fairly, and retirement is approaching as a question without a verified income or an affordable date yet.

say: I'd keep **small useful aids** and proper checks without needing another grand software announcement.
I'd prefer **colleagues getting home** on time to a poster about the future of work.
think: Our **work and money** feel secure, with covering wages, room after costs and fourteen months saved.
Our **later retirement question** remains unchecked without making the next ordinary wage unsafe.
do: Keep **offered paid repairs** within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures through the first year.
Continue **checked occasional wording** and existing quarterly income-and-bill reviews with Leif, without choosing a purchase or exit.
feel: **Calm about household security**, attentive to colleagues without borrowing their risks as a claim about her own income.
S0.quote: A clearer sentence can't add a test I never did.
fieldNote: Her **present security** rests on higher pay, covering wages and fourteen months saved; plentiful firms offer possibilities rather than guaranteed jobs.
Her **existing AI routine** remains checked wording only, while her ordinary electrician's licence confers neither master standing nor a funded retirement choice.

steps.text: Keep offered paid repairs within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures
Continue occasional checked wording and quarterly actual income-and-bill reviews with Leif

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small aid can be useful without a great announcement attached. Keep the accurate explanation and the proper repair check, and let the rest of the day be ordinary. I'd rather a colleague got home on time than another software poster went up in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money would feel secure. Both wages cover the rent and ordinary bills, and fourteen months saved means we can handle a normal interruption without rushing into debt. I still need to check the later retirement position, but an unanswered later question isn't a missing wage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid repairs now and through the first year, within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures. I'd continue the occasional checked wording aid and our existing quarterly review of actual income and bills with Leif. I wouldn't purchase another tool or choose an exit just to prove I'd made a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own living, and pleased to have a plain working year in view. I'd still notice if a colleague was getting a worse deal, even when our account looked comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What remains your responsibility when the wording aid is used?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The version I send has to describe the test and repair I actually completed. A clearer sentence can't add a test I never did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the reserve make leaving work a settled decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd need verified income, actual costs and a choice that worked for both of us. Fourteen months saved is time to ask properly, not a wage that lasts forever.

say: I'd separate **faster office replies** from the electrical judgement and actual time a callback requires.
I'd seek a **shared callback-pay request**, using colleagues' names only with consent.
think: My **normal repair wage** looks secure near term with physical work and a full diary.
I'm **uneasy about colleagues** and work outside the paid day, while covering wages and the reserve support our household.
do: Invite **willing colleagues** to sign agreed callback-pay wording using names only with consent; rely on terms only after written employer acceptance.
Keep **offered paid licensed repairs** within competence and safe procedures; record two weeks of callbacks before accepting changed paid-hour terms.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, using financial room to question working terms without assuming everyone can absorb unpaid time.
S1.quote: I can ask a colleague for support without spending the colleague's name.
fieldNote: Her **collective request** preserves consent and written-acceptance limits, without claiming every colleague or the employer agrees.
Her **own security** stays explicit despite distribution concerns; continuing occasional wording help is not new AI learning.

steps.text: Invite willing colleagues to sign agreed callback-pay wording; use names with consent, awaiting written employer acceptance
Keep offered paid repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures
Record two weeks of actual callbacks before accepting changed paid-hour terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bookings and written replies can speed up without a circuit testing itself. I'd ask willing colleagues to put a callback-pay request to the employer together, using names only with consent. A call that needed an electrician shouldn't disappear from the record because the first message came from software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own normal repair wage to hold over the next few years because most work remains physical and the repair diary is full. Leif's porter work also looks less directly exposed to thinking tools, while our reserve gives us room if something changes. I'm uneasy about office colleagues and work being pushed outside the paid day, not expecting our next rent payment to fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd invite willing colleagues to sign a request for paid callback records, using names only with consent and counting no agreement before written acceptance. I'd record two weeks of actual callback time before accepting changed paid-hour terms. Through the first year I'd keep offered paid repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures, with the existing occasional checked wording aid rather than a new AI learning plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the working day is being divided up, while secure about our own income. I can use that room to ask a definite question instead of assuming everyone can afford an unpaid evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a colleague did not want to join the request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a willing person's name would go on the request, and the wording would be agreed by those signing. I can ask a colleague for support without spending the colleague's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer declined the proposed terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep recording the real calls and ask what the branch could actually do next. A signed request from workers isn't a paid-time agreement from the employer.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking changes** at sixty from physical robots around sixty-three in 2031.
I'd keep **actual paid calls** visible instead of treating age as the answer to a changed working week.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** through faster planning before robots compete directly for physical repairs.
Our **fourteen-month reserve** gives options, without guaranteeing either household wage, employer purchases or an affordable retirement.
do: Invite **willing colleagues** to sign agreed callback-pay wording using names only with consent; rely on terms only after written employer acceptance.
Request **income records** and available membership advice; verify eligibility and costs before counting payments, keeping current paid repairs within licence and competence.
Check **2029 actual resources** and costs with Leif before an affordable agreed exit; count only genuine paid offers within actual safe capacity.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, facing possible household wage reductions without treating savings as endless or future payments as confirmed.
S2.quote: Nearby firms are places to ask, not jobs I have already been offered.
fieldNote: Her **fast-timeline anxiety** concerns possible paid-hour reductions and later physical competition, with the three-year separation retained for both household jobs.
Her **records and offers** require real information and affordable joint agreement, without assuming a pension entitlement, guaranteed job or grown-child contribution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028 when I'm sixty, then capable physical robots around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. The firm could change the paid time around repairs before the machines could compete for the repair itself. I'd still want the employer to answer a concrete question about calls rather than give us a speech about our age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if quicker planning allowed the firm to cover visits with fewer electricians. Later robots could affect both my repairs and Leif's porter work, but I don't know the actual purchases either employer would make. Fourteen months saved gives us a strong response, not certainty about two future wages or a retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite willing colleagues into the callback-pay request now, using names only with consent and relying on no terms until written acceptance. We'd request actual income records and available union membership advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting any payment; I'd keep current offered repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures. During 2029 Leif and I would compare actual income, costs, capacity and genuine paid offers before any affordable exit we both agreed, assuming neither a payment nor a job at sixty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible wage reductions, with enough room to make a careful plan. I'd be asking what we really had, rather than treating the reserve as either useless or endless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the many nearby firms guarantee another wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Nearby firms are places to ask, not jobs I have already been offered. I'd use an actual written offer and its costs in a decision, not the number of vans I see on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children supply the missing income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only help they offered freely and we actually agreed could count. The children have their own costs, and our savings don't give us a right to spend their future wages.

S3.quote: My present repair diary doesn't reserve a working body for sixty-six.
fieldNote: Her **lower immediate pressure** follows expected continuing wages and existing resources, without a pension entitlement or new savings created by extra time.
Her **later review** includes real costs and capacity; current repairs and shared requests guarantee neither future employment nor an affordable exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I'm sixty-three, followed by physical robots around 2034 at sixty-six. Five years lets us read the actual records while the current wage is still useful. I'd keep the callback question on the table now, not leave it until someone was explaining a smaller payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our present wages to remain steady over the next few years, with a full repair diary, Leif's physical job and fourteen months saved. I'm uneasy about what happens later, rather than expecting next month's money to go. I don't know either person's future health, confirmed income or available work at sixty-three or sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the same callback-pay request now with willing colleagues, using names only with consent and relying on nothing before written acceptance. We'd request income records and available membership advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments, while I kept current offered repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures. During 2032 we'd review actual income, costs, capacity and paid offers with Leif twice yearly before any affordable exit we both agreed, without assuming a job or retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later question, but comfortable enough to do the present work without treating it as a rescue mission. More time is useful for asking properly, not proof that the answer will be comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an income record was incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the provider to explain missing entries and keep our budget on confirmed figures meanwhile. A blank in the record is a task for us to follow up, not a payment I can quietly fill in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would current experience guarantee the same work at the later ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would still need an actual offered task, suitable ability and a safe way to do it then. My present repair diary doesn't reserve a working body for sixty-six.

fieldNote: Her **long horizon** leaves later work and retirement affordability open; continuing repairs are explicitly current, without guaranteed employment at sixty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2036 when I'm sixty-eight and robots around 2039 when I'm seventy-one. I'd still make a useful request about the paid day I have now. A longer warning shouldn't become an excuse for leaving the ordinary question unanswered for a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present repair and porter wages look secure over the next few years, and the reserve supports that confidence. I'm uneasy about the later figures, including whether either of us could or needed to do suitable paid work then. I won't count a retirement payment or a future employer just because the dates are farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite willing colleagues into the callback-pay request now, using names only with consent and relying on no terms before written acceptance. We'd request income records and available membership advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments, while I kept current offered repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures. During 2037 Leif and I would review actual income, costs, capacity and genuine paid offers before any affordable exit we both agreed, counting no assumed job at sixty-nine or help from the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later unknowns, but secure enough to enjoy the balcony and a quiet evening now. I don't need to borrow a younger colleague's whole working-life worry to take that colleague seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger colleague about your calmer near-term position?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be clear that my reserve and later horizon are my circumstances, not a promise about theirs. A fair paid-time agreement should protect a worker who has no fourteen-month cushion too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family support be automatic if the later figures showed a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only help offered freely and agreed with everyone's actual needs considered could count. Being a family doesn't make a future payment appear before we've spoken.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the paid time around repairs could shrink before we've checked another income, with physical robots following around 2031. Written callback-pay terms and available help reading actual income records would help, without pretending our strong reserve lasts forever. I'd want the same proper answer for a colleague who couldn't wait fourteen months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what happens after the customer says thank you. Sometimes there's another call, another explanation and another ten minutes that never gets counted. A finished repair can still leave an unfinished paid-time question.

headlineQuote: A finished repair can still leave an unfinished paid-time question.
portrait: Daria is **fifty-eight**, an experienced average electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs without master or crew-lead standing.
Her **higher pay** and partner Leif's porter wage cover costs, with rent, fourteen months saved and plentiful nearby electrical employers.
She keeps **occasional proven AI wording**, while seeking a shared callback-pay request that uses only consenting colleagues' names and assumes no agreement.
She checks **later resources**, costs, capacity and paid offers with Leif before affordable agreed exit, assuming no pension or children's wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink paid repair-related hours before another income is checked, with later physical robot risks around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Provide **written callback-pay terms** and available help checking actual income records, eligibility and costs rather than treating the reserve as endless.
